clinicalPearls: Periarticular disorders are common soft-tissue musculoskeletal problems affecting people of any age, arising from structures around (rather than within) the joint such as bursae, tendons, fascia, and connective-tissue bands.

Bursitis is inflammation of a synovial-lined sac; adults have over 150 bursae that ease gliding of tendons and muscles over bony prominences, and overuse, trauma, systemic disease (rheumatoid arthritis, gout), or infection can trigger inflammation.
Subacromial (subdeltoid) bursitis is the most common bursitis and frequently coexists with rotator cuff tendinitis, presenting with anterolateral shoulder pain.

Acutely inflamed olecranon or prepatellar bursitis with warmth/redness warrants aspiration with Gram stain, culture, and crystal examination to exclude infection or gout before assuming a mechanical cause.

Rotator cuff tendinitis (impingement syndrome) is the leading cause of a painful shoulder; the supraspinatus tendon is most often affected due to impingement between the humeral head and the anterior acromion/coracoacromial ligament, classically producing a painful abduction arc of 60-120 degrees.

Calcific tendinitis reflects hydroxyapatite (calcium salt) deposition within a tendon, most often the supraspinatus (involved in about 63% of cases), typically after age 40, and may be asymptomatic or cause sudden severe shoulder pain.

De Quervain's tenosynovitis involves the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis at the radial styloid; a positive Finkelstein test (thumb tucked in fist with ulnar wrist deviation) reproduces radial styloid pain.

Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) causes painful, globally restricted active and passive shoulder motion, usually without intrinsic joint disease, and is associated with diabetes, thyroid disease, chronic pulmonary disease, and prior myocardial infarction.

Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) arises from repetitive resisted wrist extension/supination; most patients are injured by activities other than tennis such as pulling weeds, carrying briefcases, or using a screwdriver.

Plantar fasciitis classically causes severe heel pain with the first steps in the morning or after rest, easing with initial activity then worsening with prolonged weight-bearing; tenderness localizes to the medial calcaneal attachment of the fascia.

Drug-induced tendinopathy is increasingly recognized, with quinolones, glucocorticoids, aromatase inhibitors, and statins implicated; the Achilles tendon is most often affected and rupture can be the presenting event.

Yergason's test (pain on resisted forearm supination with the elbow at 90 degrees) supports bicipital tendinitis; biceps tendon rupture in older patients may be painless and recognized by a retracted bulge of the long head.
harrison.pathophysiology: These are disorders of the soft tissues surrounding joints rather than the synovial joint itself. Bursitis is synovial inflammation of a bursa from frictional overuse, trauma, systemic inflammatory/crystal disease, or infection. Tendinopathies (rotator cuff, bicipital, patellar, epicondylar, De Quervain's) result from mechanical impingement and repetitive resisted loading producing microtears, inflammation, and degeneration at tendon insertions; the supraspinatus is uniquely vulnerable to impingement beneath the acromion. Calcific tendinitis is caused by hydroxyapatite deposition within tendon substance through poorly understood phases of calcification that can incite acute inflammation. Adhesive capsulitis features a thickened shoulder capsule with mild chronic inflammatory infiltrate and fibrosis, often after a period of immobility. Plantar fasciitis arises at the fascial origin on the medial calcaneal tuberosity from cumulative loading. Drug-induced tendinopathies have an unknown mechanism but are linked to specific drug classes.
additionalDifferentials: Cervical radiculopathy referring to the shoulder
Intraarticular knee pathology (osteoarthritis, meniscal injury) versus periarticular knee pain
infectionMimics: Septic arthritis presenting as periarticular pain and swelling
nonInfectiousMimics: Calcium pyrophosphate or apatite crystal deposition
Rheumatoid or inflammatory arthritis involving periarticular structures
Referred pain from intraarticular degenerative joint disease
additionalInvestigations: History and directed physical examination (often sufficient for diagnosis)
Provocative maneuvers (painful abduction arc, drop-arm test, Finkelstein test, Yergason's test)
Bursal aspiration with Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis when infection or gout is suspected
Ultrasound (for bursitis, tendinitis, rotator cuff tears, calcific deposits, plantar fascia thickening, and guided injection)
Plain radiographs (may show tendon calcification or incidental heel spurs)
MRI (sensitive for rotator cuff tears, tendon integrity, and plantar fasciitis when diagnosis is unclear)
redFlags: Acutely warm, red, tender bursa suggesting septic bursitis or gout requiring aspiration
Weakness of abduction/external rotation or a positive drop-arm test suggesting a rotator cuff tear
Acute tendon rupture (e.g., Achilles in drug-induced tendinopathy, biceps in active patients)
Globally restricted active and passive shoulder motion suggesting adhesive capsulitis rather than a focal tendinitis
Periarticular pain in the setting of systemic disease (rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, thyroid disease) prompting evaluation of the underlying condition
harrison.prognosis: Most periarticular disorders are self-limited and respond to conservative measures. Adhesive capsulitis usually improves spontaneously over 1-3 years, though many patients retain some residual loss of shoulder motion. More than 80% of plantar fasciitis cases resolve within 12 months. Calcific tendinitis is largely self-limited. Rotator cuff tears vary in outcome depending on tear size, chronicity, pain, functional loss, and coexisting osteoarthritis.
pitfalls: Anserine bursitis is a frequently overlooked periarticular cause of knee pain.
Assuming inflamed olecranon or prepatellar bursitis is mechanical without excluding infection or gout by aspiration.
Mislabeling globally restricted shoulder motion as simple tendinitis when it is adhesive capsulitis.
Attributing heel pain to a radiographic heel spur, which is of little diagnostic significance in plantar fasciitis.
Overlooking medication as a cause of tendon pain or rupture (drug-induced tendinopathy), and reintroducing the offending agent.
Confusing iliopsoas bursitis pain with pain originating within the hip joint itself.
harrison.severityClassification: No formal grading system; rotator cuff tears are clinically characterized as acute, subacute, or chronic and as partial- or full-thickness, with management guided by tear severity, symptom duration, pain, functional loss, and coexisting osteoarthritis.
